title: Shami Says He Is Still at His Peak and Will Fight for an India Return
excerpt: Overlooked for the New Zealand tour after more than 20 months out, the 36-year-old fast bowler says he is fully fit, has heard nothing from the new selectors, and will press his case through Bengal's Ranji season.
body:
• Mohammed Shami, overlooked for India's Test and ODI squads for the New Zealand tour, says he is still at his peak and fully fit after more than 20 months out of the national side.
  • The 36-year-old has had no contact from the selectors since Ajit Agarkar's tenure ended and Pragyan Ojha took over as chair, and plans to press his case through a full domestic season with Bengal.
  • Shami sat out Bengal's Ranji Trophy match against Services, a game the spinners dominated, after bowling 17.3 overs for four wickets against Delhi the previous round.
  • His route back is performances, not statements: keep playing, keep taking wickets, and be ready if the call comes before the 2027 ODI World Cup.

Mohammed Shami has not played for India since March 2025. Left out again this week, when the squads for the New Zealand tour were announced without his name in either the Test or the ODI party, the fast bowler gave the only answer available to him. He is fit, he is bowling, and he is not done.

"I am still at my peak. There is no point beating around the bush," Shami told reporters, according to Madhyamam. He said he had bowled for an hour and a half in training on the day he spoke, with no discomfort.

The Silence From the Selectors

Shami's absence stretched past 20 months while the selection leadership changed around him. Ajit Agarkar's tenure as chief selector ended earlier this month and Pragyan Ojha has taken over. Shami says there has been no direct contact from the new committee, and he has framed it without bitterness: out of the side and without a central contract, he does not expect a call explaining himself.

What he can control is the domestic season. "I'm always positive and focused on performing well in every match I play. I want to keep playing as many matches as possible because that helps me maintain my physical momentum, improve my game, and sharpen my skills," Shami told ANI, in comments reported by Daily Prabhat. "What more can I do than keep playing and giving my best?"

"I am still at my peak. There is no point beating around the bush."

— Mohammed Shami, India fast bowler

The Missed Match That Started the Talk

The latest round of speculation began when Shami missed Bengal's second-round Ranji Trophy match against Services, two days after the New Zealand squads were named. Bengal won by 60 runs on a surface at the Air Force Ground in Palam where spinners took 39 of the 40 wickets, a pitch that offered seamers almost nothing.

Bengal head coach Laxmi Ratan Shukla dismissed the fitness reading entirely. "Shami is fit, he was rested. He bowled a lot of overs against Delhi last round. He himself asked to be rested," Shukla said, in comments reported by Cricket Addictor. Against Delhi, Shami had taken four for 30 in 17.3 overs, including nine maidens.

Shami himself pushed back on the idea that spell lengths in domestic cricket reveal anything about his body. Spell lengths, he argued, follow the match situation, the pitch and the captain's call, not an outside observer's assumption about what a fast bowler should be able to bowl.

Why the Door Is Not Closed

The context working in Shami's favour is that veteran pace recalls are happening around him. Bhuvneshwar Kumar, 36, has been recalled for the New Zealand T20Is, a selection Shami welcomed, saying his fellow seamer should have been given a chance earlier. Shami remains India's fastest bowler to 200 ODI wickets, and his record in global tournaments is the strongest argument he owns.

He has also stepped away from social media, saying his time now goes to training, practice and match play. For diaspora fans watching the New Zealand tour, the question is no longer whether Shami wants one more run at a World Cup. It is whether a season of Ranji wickets can force a selection committee that has not called him to change its mind.

What's Next

Shami's calendar is Bengal's calendar: a full Ranji season, wicket by wicket. Every five-wicket haul will restart the conversation. The selectors have made no promise, and Shami has stopped asking for one in public. The ball, as he keeps pointing out, is doing the talking.
